newsitem.title: USA: Theory on Darwin's illness draws debate.
newsitem.headline: Theory on Darwin's illness draws debate.

text.p: A theory claiming that scientist Charles Darwin suffered from a panic disorder and phobia that often turns its victims into recluses provoked a debate in a prominent medical journal on Tuesday.
His health problems really came from a parasite which infected his stomach during his travels, two experts suggested. A third said Darwin's inner ear may have been the culprit.

The issue was raised in January when two researchers at the University of Iowa College of Medicine published a paper saying that Darwin, whose travels and resulting theory of evolution altered the course of science, suffered from panic disorder and agoraphobia -- a disorder that often makes people fearful of leaving their homes.

Thomas Barloon and Russell Noyes suggested in their paper that Darwin's ironic condition changed his life style from that of a world-wide collector to a recluse and in the process helped him focus on and complete his "Origin of the Species."

Their paper was published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, which on Tuesday printed four letters from various experts commenting on or challenging the speculation, as well as a response from the original authors.
Another expert suggested in his response that Darwin's "well-known flatulence" and his reports of constant stomach problems point to Chagas disease, a parasitic infection spread by insects.
Another writer suggested that Darwin, who lived from 1809 to 1882, possibly had Chagas disease and panic disorder but not agoraphobia.
A third writer said his diagnosis pointed to Meniere's disease, an inner-ear condition that leads to vertigo and other problems.

The writers of the original report replied that certain elements of Darwin's condition still point to agorophobia, but they admitted that the mystery surrounding his illness is likely to remain a subject of debate.
